newsitem.title: USA: Gold steadies, finally gets facts after rumors of sales.
newsitem.headline: Gold steadies, finally gets facts after rumors of sales.

text.p: Gold prices held steady Monday amid relief at getting some facts after months of guessing about central bank sales of bullion, which had driven the market to the lowest levels in more than three years.

On New York's Commodity Exchange, the active February gold contract closed 50 cents lower at $359.70 an ounce after rallying early to $361.70 on the Dutch Central Bank's announcement that it had sold 300 metric tons of gold from its reserves last year.

But the market showed little reaction to a later statement by Bundesbank President Hans Teitmayer, that the Group of 10 central banks saw no need to sell gold for the time being to boost national revenues.
The market welcomed some facts about central bank selling of bullion, which recently drove gold to $358 an ounce, a level unseen since early October 1993, when it hovered at $350.

"People were a little unsure as to whether (the Dutch sales) were bullish or bearish," a bullion trader said. "Short term it may be constructive because now we can see why the market's come off $30. It's out of the way now," he said.
Rumours of a sale from a central bank of around 10 million ounces or 300 tons had circulated for weeks and were a key factor behind gold's weakness.

The G10 statement that the countries should enjoy economic growth in 1997 and 1998 and their central banks see no need to sell gold reserves to boost national revenues "for the time being" generated more confusion, dealers said.
"People aren't reacting to it because they don't understand what it really means," one trader said.
The 11 members of the so-called G10 are Belgium, Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, Sweden, the United States and Switzerland.
